[2025 summer phd math-stat — problem 1]

Part III, Problem 1 (25 pts). Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. from a one-parameter exponential family $p(x \mid \theta) = h(x)\exp\{\eta(\theta) T(x) - B(\theta)\}$, with $\eta(\theta)$ monotonically increasing and $\sum_i T(X_i)$ continuous.
(i) Construct the UMP test for $H_0 : \theta \le \theta_0$ vs $H_1 : \theta > \theta_0$.
(ii) Prove the test in (i) is uniformly most powerful.
(iii) Prove or disprove the existence of a UMP test for $H_0 : \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1 : \theta \ne \theta_0$.

response.text:
Let  

\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i).
\]

The joint density is

\[
f_\theta(x_1,\dots,x_n)
=\prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)\exp\{\eta(\theta)S-nB(\theta)\}.
\]

Thus for \(\theta_2>\theta_1\),

\[
\frac{f_{\theta_2}}{f_{\theta_1}}
=\exp\{[\eta(\theta_2)-\eta(\theta_1)]S-n[B(\theta_2)-B(\theta_1)]\}.
\]

Since \(\eta\) is increasing, this likelihood ratio is an increasing function of \(S\). Hence the family has a monotone likelihood ratio in \(S\).

Assume a fixed nontrivial level \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Because \(S\) is continuous, no boundary randomization is needed.

---

## (i) UMP test for \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\) versus \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\)

Let \(F_{\theta_0}\) be the distribution function of \(S\) under \(\theta_0\). Choose \(c_\alpha\) such that

\[
P_{\theta_0}(S>c_\alpha)=\alpha,
\]

equivalently \(F_{\theta_0}(c_\alpha)=1-\alpha\).

Define the test

\[
\phi_\alpha(X_1,\dots,X_n)
=
\mathbf 1\{S>c_\alpha\}.
\]

So the UMP level-\(\alpha\) test rejects \(H_0\) when

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n T(X_i)>c_\alpha.
\]

---

## (ii) Proof that the test is UMP

We prove two things: first that \(\phi_\alpha\) has level \(\alpha\), and then that it is uniformly most powerful.

### Step 1: Level \(\alpha\)

Because the family has monotone likelihood ratio in \(S\), the distribution of \(S\) is stochastically increasing in \(\theta\). In particular, if \(\theta_1<\theta_2\), then for every \(c\),

\[
P_{\theta_1}(S>c)\le P_{\theta_2}(S>c).
\]

Therefore, for every \(\theta\le \theta_0\),

\[
P_\theta(S>c_\alpha)\le P_{\theta_0}(S>c_\alpha)=\alpha.
\]

Hence

\[
\sup_{\theta\le \theta_0}E_\theta[\phi_\alpha]
=
\sup_{\theta\le \theta_0}P_\theta(S>c_\alpha)
=
\alpha.
\]

Thus \(\phi_\alpha\) is a level-\(\alpha\) test.

### Step 2: Most powerful against each fixed \(\theta_1>\theta_0\)

Fix \(\theta_1>\theta_0\). The likelihood ratio for testing the simple null \(\theta=\theta_0\) against the simple alternative \(\theta=\theta_1\) is

\[
\frac{f_{\theta_1}}{f_{\theta_0}}
=
\exp\{[\eta(\theta_1)-\eta(\theta_0)]S-n[B(\theta_1)-B(\theta_0)]\}.
\]

Since \(\eta(\theta_1)>\eta(\theta_0)\), this is an increasing function of \(S\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test for \(\theta_0\) versus \(\theta_1\) rejects for large values of this likelihood ratio, equivalently for large values of \(S\). The rejection region must therefore be of the form

\[
\{S>c\}.
\]

To have size \(\alpha\) under \(\theta_0\), we must choose \(c=c_\alpha\). Hence the Neyman–Pearson most powerful test for \(\theta_0\) versus this fixed \(\theta_1>\theta_0\) is exactly

\[
\phi_\alpha=\mathbf 1\{S>c_\alpha\}.
\]

Now let \(\psi\) be any level-\(\alpha\) test for the composite null \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\). Then in particular

\[
E_{\theta_0}[\psi]\le \alpha.
\]

By the Neyman–Pearson lemma,

\[
E_{\theta_1}[\psi]\le E_{\theta_1}[\phi_\alpha].
\]

Since this holds for every \(\theta_1>\theta_0\), \(\phi_\alpha\) is uniformly most powerful for \(H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\) versus \(H_1:\theta>\theta_0\).

This is the Karlin–Rubin theorem applied to this one-parameter exponential family.

---

## (iii) Existence of a UMP test for \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\) versus \(H_1:\theta\neq \theta_0\)

In general, no nontrivial UMP level-\(\alpha\) test exists for the two-sided alternative.

Assume \(\theta_0\) is an interior point of the parameter space, so that there exist alternatives on both sides of \(\theta_0\). Suppose, toward a contradiction, that a UMP level-\(\alpha\) test \(\phi\) exists for

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\theta\neq \theta_0.
\]

Take some \(\theta_+>\theta_0\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the unique most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test of

\[
\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{versus}\quad
\theta=\theta_+
\]

rejects for large \(S\), namely

\[
\phi_+(X)=\mathbf 1\{S>c_+\},
\]

where

\[
P_{\theta_0}(S>c_+)=\alpha.
\]

Since a UMP test must in particular be most powerful against this fixed \(\theta_+\), we must have

\[
\phi=\phi_+
\quad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Now take \(\theta_-<\theta_0\). Then

\[
\frac{f_{\theta_-}}{f_{\theta_0}}
=
\exp\{[\eta(\theta_-)-\eta(\theta_0)]S-n[B(\theta_-)-B(\theta_0)]\}
\]

is a decreasing function of \(S\). Therefore, by the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the unique most powerful level-\(\alpha\) test of

\[
\theta=\theta_0
\quad\text{versus}\quad
\theta=\theta_-
\]

rejects for small \(S\), namely

\[
\phi_-(X)=\mathbf 1\{S<c_-\},
\]

where

\[
P_{\theta_0}(S<c_-)=\alpha.
\]

Again, a UMP test would have to satisfy

\[
\phi=\phi_-
\quad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

Thus we would need

\[
\mathbf 1\{S>c_+\}
=
\mathbf 1\{S<c_-\}
\quad P_{\theta_0}\text{-a.s.}
\]

But this is impossible for \(0<\alpha<1\). Indeed, both sets have \(P_{\theta_0}\)-probability \(\alpha\), but one is an upper-tail set and the other is a lower-tail set. Since \(S\) is continuous, they cannot agree up to a null set.

Therefore no nontrivial UMP level-\(\alpha\) test exists for

\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\theta\neq \theta_0.
\]

Only trivial exceptions exist, such as \(\alpha=0\) or \(\alpha=1\), or the case where \(\theta_0\) is a boundary point so that the problem is effectively one-sided.
